story.headline: Oil turned higher after Iran said the US hit one of its bases, lifting US yields and the dollar. France's unrest kept the euro near its lows, while China's growth beat lifted the Aussie.

reads.policy: Nearly every central bank is holding this month and pointing at a hike later, so the race is about who moves first. The Bank of England looks closest, while Canada's soft core inflation and Japan's caution pushed their next hikes further out. Currencies whose banks look ready to act, like the pound, have the edge.
reads.growth: China grew a little faster than expected, which helped the currencies that sell to it, like the Australian dollar. In the US, high mortgage rates are hurting housing, and Canadian firms grew gloomier after trade talks collapsed. Growth is uneven, but it isn't yet weak enough to change central banks' plans.
reads.inflation: Canada's inflation came in a little soft, and its core measures are back below the 2% target, so energy is doing most of the work there. But people now expect more inflation, and oil turned higher again today, which keeps central banks wary. This week's UK, New Zealand and Japan reports decide how much more pressure they face.
reads.risk: The calm broke in the afternoon when Iran said the US struck one of its naval bases, and the Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi oil sites. France's unrest weighed on European markets, while US tech stocks bounced. Fear is now coming from two places at once, which keeps a floor under safe havens like the franc.
reads.tot: Oil fell in the morning on the Russia sanctions waiver, then turned higher on the new Gulf attacks. Expensive oil helps exporters like Canada and costs importers like Japan and the euro area. It also lifts yields, which is why gold fell on a day with more conflict news.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds are betting most heavily against the Canadian dollar and added to bets against the euro, which France's trouble rewarded today. They still lean toward the Australian dollar while long-term investors bet against it, so a bad turn in risk mood could hit it fast. In the yen and the Aussie, the two groups disagree.
reads.fiscal: France is the fiscal story this week: investors sold French bonds and stocks together, which signals worry about its finances rather than ordinary caution. That pushes the euro down through higher borrowing costs. The US deficit is large too, but for now it shows up in higher yields rather than a weaker dollar.

fed.summary: The Fed is expected to hold in October and is likely to hike in December. Higher oil pushed US yields up today, which keeps the dollar supported.
fed.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike likely.
fed.why: Inflation ran hot last week and oil is climbing again, which keeps rate-hike talk alive. Soft housing is a reason for caution, but not yet enough to change the plan.
fed.watch: The Fed is in its quiet period until the October 28 decision. Until then, oil and yields set the tone.

boc.summary: Canada's core inflation fell below 2%, so the Bank of Canada looks set to hold on October 28. Rising inflation expectations keep a later hike alive, which limits the loonie's downside.
boc.priced: October hike: about 1 in 4; December: likely.
boc.why: Cooling core prices and a weak job market argue for waiting. People expecting more inflation, and oil near $100, argue against dropping hike talk.
boc.watch: The October 28 decision and its statement: whether the bank leans on today's cool prices or tomorrow's expected ones.

rbnz.summary: The RBNZ is split between hiking and holding on October 28. Wednesday's inflation report will decide it, and the kiwi is waiting.
rbnz.priced: October 28: close call between hike and hold.
rbnz.why: Strong business activity points to a hike. A wider trade gap and cooler services point to waiting.
rbnz.watch: New Zealand's inflation figure on Wednesday. A hot number tips the bank toward a hike.

ecb.summary: The ECB is expected to hold in October and lean toward a December hike. France's budget trouble is weighing on the euro more than rate hopes are helping it.
ecb.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike likely.
ecb.why: Inflation is at a three-year high, so a December hike is still the base case. French bond stress is the main worry.
ecb.watch: France's budget vote on Tuesday and Moody's review on Friday. Lagarde speaks on Wednesday.

boj.summary: The BoJ is signalling more hikes, most likely in December rather than October. Until then the yen stays weak because US rates are so much higher.
boj.why: Ueda said underlying inflation is close to the 2% goal. But inflation is still below the bank's own forecast, so there is no rush.
boj.watch: Japan's inflation report on Friday. Also the yen near 160 per dollar, a level where Japan has stepped in before.

rba.summary: The RBA hints rates may not be high enough yet, keeping a November hike possible. The Aussie is leaning more on China than on the RBA right now.
rba.priced: November hike: about 1 in 3; December: a coin flip.
rba.why: Kent said the neutral rate may be rising and inflation is stuck. He also said the job market is loosening faster than expected.
rba.watch: Australia's quarterly inflation report on October 28, the key test for a November hike.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates on November 5. That support helped the pound to a 17-month high against the euro.
boe.why: Inflation is expected to rise again, and the bank has signalled it will act. The open question is whether it keeps going in December.
boe.watch: UK wage data on Tuesday and inflation on Wednesday. The budget follows on October 28.

snb.summary: The SNB holds at zero and could cut in December because Swiss inflation is very low. The franc moves on outside fear, and today it gained against the euro.
snb.priced: Holding at 0%; a December cut is possible.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is very soft, so the bank has no reason to tighten. The franc's moves come from France and the Middle East, not Swiss news.
snb.watch: Thursday's write-up of the SNB's last meeting. A rise in European or Gulf stress would lift the franc regardless.
